cells.tense: You are at the door right now and your hands are open for what is arriving.
cells.ask: Before you pick up the next thing that arrives, say out loud who it's for and what it costs you. Keep the same load and drop the strain.
cells.core:
You're standing at the door and your hands are open. What's arriving gets met without being squeezed or dropped, and your arms stay steady while the thing is still being what it is. That isn't softness and it isn't force. The grip and the give are both doing their job.

You know when to absorb and when to let it move through, and it costs you almost nothing, which is how you can tell it's working. What this steadiness can feed next is the part that reaches other people — not by taking their load, but by standing next to them while they carry it. Pick the next thing that arrives and say who it's for. You can set it down whenever you want.
cells.sheetLine: You hold what arrives without tightening around it.
cells.verb: bearing what must be borne without hardening
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving comes in from outside

cells.tense: You are bracing for something further out, and the bracing has become how you stand.
cells.ask: Pick the one weight you'd reach for first if the worst arrived, and put it down for today. If the day actually calls for it, you can pick it back up.
cells.core:
Somewhere out ahead is a pressure you can feel coming, and your body is already shaped for it. The grip that was meant for one moment is on all the time now, so what arrives meets resistance before it's even here. The strength got wider than it needed to be, and what that costs is the give in your hands.

The way back is fair weighing — not a score to settle, just whatever fits the actual weight in front of you. The difference between carrying and clamping down is smaller than it feels. Pick what you'd reach for first if things got hard, and leave it on the ground today. Nothing about the load changes. Only how long your hands are clenched.

cells.tense: You learned once that holding something up was not safe, and the lesson is still deciding what you touch now.
cells.ask: Pick one small thing arriving this week and say out loud that you're not taking it. Nothing gets carried, and nothing gets fixed.
cells.core:
What arrives at the door meets a decision that was already made. You can still steady things without meaning to — that hasn't gone anywhere — but it doesn't get picked up. Somehow setting something down got filed next to dropping it, so the hands stay at your sides and the thing waits.

What moves this is release, not more effort. Let one thing that isn't yours go through without your arms around it, and notice that nothing collapsed when it did. You don't have to feel stronger before you try it. Say the sentence, hold the line, and let the next thing find its own place to land.
cells.sheetLine: Holding feels like the risk now, so nothing gets held.
cells.verb: bearing what must be borne without hardening
cells.place: at the threshold where what's arriving comes in from outside

cells.tense: The bearing is already happening in the room, and it's going down in your account as something else.
cells.ask: Take one thing you call just getting through and say aloud that bearing it was a strength. Name it for what it is, once.
cells.core:
You are already carrying what's coming in — waking up with it, making room for it, staying upright while it's here — and none of that registers as strength from where you sit. It reads as the price of doing anything at all. But you do it, the same way your hands know the shape of a thing before you look.

What brings this back is pointing at what was there earlier, before it looked ordinary. Name one small light: one time you stood firm, one time you were the one who stayed. That isn't decoration on the day. It's the part of you that's been doing the work the whole time.
cells.sheetLine: The bearing is already yours, and you're not counting it.

attempts.check: The record gives the mechanism and the family line, not this person's history, so any sentence that says what happened at a door, who stood there, or how long the bracing has run is mine and not the record's. A reader could reasonably say the fortitude is just an ordinary day's stamina and the reflex never fired — the asks still work if that is true, because each is one act they can try and abandon. The sentence that serves me more than them is any version of 'you have always been the strong one,' so I left it out.
